ChIJ22I78SsgZIgRcEMjlokAjXs.home: Adaptive Reuse in the heart of Historic Lebanon, TN The Mill at Lebanon is an adaptive reuse project converting the former Lebanon Woolen Mills into a mixed use facility encompassing offices, event spaces and other creative spaces. The Lebanon Woolen Mills began operation in 1908 and ceased operations in 1998. It has since been renovated and preserved and welcomes you to visit our very special space. From unique shopping and local dining to wellness, arts, and professional services, each tenant brings something distinct to the experience. Whether visiting for a class, a cup of coffee, a creative workshop, or simply to explore, there is always something new to uncover. Take a walk through The Mill and see how this historic space continues to evolve as a hub of activity, connection, and local entrepreneurship. From intimate gatherings to grand celebrations, The Mill at Lebanon offers a one-of-a-kind setting for every occasion. With a variety of unique spaces and the ability to host everything from weddings and milestone celebrations to corporate events, markets, and community gatherings, The Mill blends historic character with modern flexibility. Whether planning an elegant reception, a large-scale fundraiser, or a creative event experience, each space provides a memorable backdrop designed to bring people together. ChIJ22I78SsgZIgRcEMjlokAjXs.about: “The story of the Lebanon Woolen Mills is the story of a woolen thread. A thread that has entwined itself into the hearts and lives of thousands of persons; one that has bound the people of Lebanon together through prosperity and depression, through gladness and sorrow.” Excerpt from the 50th Anniversary Yearbook 1958 In 1908, Dr. Edgerton founded the Lebanon Woolen Mills in Lebanon, Tennessee. Legend holds that Dr. Edgerton experienced a high degree of frustration as he was compensated for his services with chickens, garden goods, and various other items of barter. Dr. Edgerton observed a proliferation of sheep farmers in the area and felt that a woolen mill would provide employment for the community. He started the Lebanon Woolen Mills in 1908 and it remained in operation until 1998 when it was closed for good. Throughout its life it became the largest employer in Lebanon and multiple generations of many families relied on the Mill for their livelihood. Under new ownership, an adaptive reuse vision unfolded to convert the historic buildings from their original purpose of manufacturing to a mixed use complex incorporating retail, entertainment, office, and residential components. The complex consists of approximately 200,000 square-foot of buildings on 15 acres, just one block from Lebanon’s Downtown Square. ChIJ16fXQVxmZIgRUZ3oRZEWL-8.about: Since 1957, Nashville City Club has been the premier membership club for Nashville's leading business professionals and executives. WITH MORE THAN 65 YEARS OF RICH AND CELEBRATED HISTORY, NASHVILLE CITY CLUB HAS CONTINUALLY SOUGHT TO FOSTER A VIBRANT AND PASSIONATE COMMUNITY, BOTH WITHIN THE CLUB AND THROUGHOUT THE EXCITING CITY OF NASHVILLE. WITH A FOCUS ON SUPERIOR SERVICE, DINING AND ELEVATED AMENITIES, BOTH CURRENT AND FUTURE MEMBERS CAN EXPERIENCE A REFINED, YET RELAXED, ENVIRONMENT THAT FEELS EQUALLY AS SOPHISTICATED AS IT IS WELCOMING. THROUGHOUT ITS YEARS, THE CITY CLUB HAS HOSTED PRESIDENTS AND VICE-PRESIDENTS, DIGNITARIES, POLITICIANS AND CELEBRITIES, AS WELL AS LOCAL LEGENDS ACROSS NUMEROUS PROFESSIONAL FIELDS INCLUDING POLITICS, LAW, HEALTHCARE, ENTERTAINMENT, REAL ESTATE, AND TECH. Circa 1825. Just a few hundred yards from Old Hickory Lake lies historic Spring Haven Mansion. Steeped in history and charm, the gorgeous two-story home sits on beautiful tree-enshrouded grounds. The property includes a cabin, a natural spring, spring house, original smoke house, and barn. Built in the early 1800s by Polly Wagnon and her husband John — a close friend and personal physician of Andrew Jackson — the mansion shares many design elements with Jackson's nearby home, the Hermitage. Jackson was a frequent visitor to the property. Today, Spring Haven is one of the most popular Nashville-area wedding venues and romantic elopement destinations. "Our guests are still talking about how beautiful the mansion and grounds were and how lovely our wedding was." Formal Parlors, a Cabin Circa 1800 and a Terrace for 125 Tucked away and surrounded by lush foliage, Spring Haven transports you back in time. Featuring formal parlors, a unique cabin circa 1800, and private dressing areas, the Mansion provides the perfect setting for your wedding and reception. For couples who prefer an outdoor venue, your ceremony can be held on the impeccably landscaped grounds. Your guests can flow from the Mansion onto the covered terrace — perfect for an alfresco cocktail hour. A gorgeous two-story home with formal parlors, dressing rooms, and intimate indoor ceremony spaces. ChIJ57KrqKE4ZIgR6CgGyPDHgeo.about: The story of the mansion, and what still stands on its grounds Spring Haven was built in the early 1800s, around 1825, as the home of John Wagnon and his wife, Polly. John was Andrew Jackson’s personal physician as well as a close friend, and Jackson came to the house often. Set the mansion beside the Hermitage, Jackson’s own home a short way off, and you’ll find many of the same design elements. The two-story house stands on tree-shaded grounds at 1 Spring Haven Ct in Hendersonville, a few hundred yards from Old Hickory Lake and 22 miles from downtown Nashville. Four more buildings stand around it. Older than the mansion itself: it dates to around 1800. A natural spring, with its spring house beside it. The original smoke house, and a barn that couples use as a photo backdrop. These days the house hosts weddings, elopements and corporate gatherings. Inside are formal parlors and private dressing areas. Outside, the covered terrace holds up to 125 guests, with uplighting, a handcrafted wooden bar and, on cool fall nights, fire lamps. Weddings book as one of three collections , for up to 40, 100 or 125 guests. Smaller ceremonies use one of five elopement packages . Tours are private and take in the mansion and the grounds. About letting women know they were not invisible in their grief. But over time, The Angel Project began to grow beyond simply being seen. It also became about encouragement and gently speaking truth in seasons where strength feels thin. At the heart of this ministry is the belief that Scripture is not only meant to be read, but carried. Hidden in our hearts. Returned to in the quiet moments when faith feels fragile and the path forward feels uncertain. Throughout Scripture, physical objects were used to mark remembrance, covenant, and reflection. In that same spirit, each bracelet is created as a tangible reminder of God’s Word, paired intentionally with verses that speak life, hope, and endurance. Whether gifted in a season of loss or chosen as a personal reminder of faith, every piece offered through The Angel Project is created with prayer, intention, and care. ChIJ9-ws6T6BY4gRtMlZx8uH4Fk.about: Graystone Quarry was originally used as the limestone source for Interstate 65 from Columbia, TN to Nashville, TN, literally paving the way to Music City. Early in 2014, Graystone Quarry was purchased and began the year long process of being cleaned up and re-zoned to accommodate an event venue and live music amphitheater. ChIJBzVLwUSjZogRDPl386vLRJs.home: Middle Tennessee Family owned and operated Ranch hospitality, from our family to yours. Family owned and family run — the same hands that built the barn greet you at the gate. From your first tour to the last dance, we handle the details while you and your guests enjoy the lawn, the saloon and the wide-open sky. Every corner of Stonewall was made to be photographed and remembered. Southern charm wrapped in western luxury, with light pouring through every window. A vintage saloon and cigar lounge for the toast before the celebration. A classic Airstream reborn as a rolling sanctuary of libations. Hickory & Peaches deliver cold beer through the crowd with unmatched flair. The ranch changes with the calendar — evergreen and candlelight in December, warm amber and dried wheat in October. A dedicated seasonal collection is being styled now. Evening, and welcome to Stonewall Ranch. I'm Belle — I can tell you about the suites, the Airstream bar, the beer burros, or how a day out here comes together. What brings you our way?
ChIJBzVLwUSjZogRDPl386vLRJs.about: In 2021, we said goodbye to our Nana, the dreamer who always spoke of one day owning land together with her family. In 2023, united by her memory and fueled by her vision, we made that dream a reality. We poured our love, sweat and hope into raw land and built what is now Stonewall Ranch — a wedding and event venue rooted in legacy and designed to celebrate life's most meaningful moments. Stonewall Ranch is a tribute to love, family, hard work and the power of coming together to build something special for generations to come. Around the ranch you will find the original stone walls that have stood here for generations. We waited to name the ranch until we all walked the property line and learned the land. We poured our hearts — and a lot of elbow grease — into rehabbing and preserving them, because they are more than walls, they are storytellers. Our mom Angel really took lead on preserving these walls and spent so much time on them; they are her babies. We believe the walls were originally built by Irish settlers for their crops and livestock. Every single stone holds a piece of the past, and now they can be a small part of your forever. Long before music filled the room, couples exchanged vows, or guests gathered beneath its reclaimed wood ceilings, this building belonged to another Nashville era. Built in 1929, it first operated as the Se-Ling Hosiery Mill, where many people from the surrounding neighborhood came to work each day. Over the decades, it became home to Genesco and later Madison Mill—its brick walls quietly witnessing generations of craftsmanship, ambition, and change. Eventually, the machines stopped and the building fell silent. When Tamay Ozari purchased the property in 1996 for his restaurant-equipment company, he found a neglected structure filled with pigeons—but also something that could not be recreated: history, character, and possibility. Years later, when potential buyers planned to replace it with apartments, he chose not to sell. Rather than watch a Nashville landmark disappear, he decided to preserve it and return it to the community. The restoration gave the old factory a new purpose. During the post war period, he met a lovely Japanese lady, Mitsue Matsubara, whom he courted, married and brought back to Milton, landing there in 1953. He quickly found a roughly 220 acre farm located on Manson Pike on the west side of Murfreesboro which he purchased and began a Grade “B” dairy operation. The land was rough and he spent the next 4 decades improving it, along with his herd, clearing trees, laying fences and “bustin’ up rocks” the old fashioned way with a sledge hammer and pick axe. Following his service in support of Operation Desert Storm, Todd completed his enlistment and returned to his home state of Tennessee. Throughout the 1990s and 2000s, Todd continued to build his career as a DJ while expanding his technical and creative skill set. He became a licensed skydiver and videographer and worked in computer and internet support industries. As the owner of an internet café in Knoxville, Tennessee, Todd was an early adopter of digital DJ technology, transitioning from traditional vinyl and CDs to digital media. In 2013, Todd relocated to the Nashville area, where he continues to provide professional DJ services for a wide range of events. His experience includes community events such as the American Heart Association heart walk, restaurant and club residencies, local church gatherings, and numerous weddings at Nashville area hotels and venues. ChIJT4DDw1Z9ZIgR6osF-5Iek2o.home: Nestled in the hills just outside Nashville, the Castle sits on a unique plot of land made up of sprawling grass fields and a cedar forest creeping up a limestone hill in the back. Maintained walking trails lead to the top of the hill where incredible vistas of the valley below can be found. The Castle itself has been standing for nearly 100 years and has served as one of Nashville’s premier commercial recording studios for the past 37. The interior is just as remarkable as its exterior and features several multipurpose rooms, lounges, and a full kitchen. To see more of the space and the grounds hit the button below. The Castle was built between 1929 and 1932 by Chicago mobster and bookie John P. Welch to serve as a hideout and resting spot while traveling between Chicago and Florida. Being an avid gambler, Welch would often throw lavish (and illegal) gambling parties on the premises. To this purpose he was sure to include in the design of the building a hidden passageway that led to an underground mushroom cellar intended to hide “guests”. After Welch died in 1945 the Castle was sold and turned into a gourmet restaurant for a stint in the late 1940’s. During this period it played host to several big stars of the time, including Bob Hope, Spencer Tracy, and Betty Grable. Over the next 30 years the property served as a riding academy for a time and later as a residence until it was purchased in 1979 by the Nuyens family, a European bluegrass group. A few years later, in 1983, Jozef Nuyens founded Castle Recording Studios. Since then, more than 500 gold and platinum artists across all genres have recorded breakout albums here at the Castle. ChIJTdaqdpB5ZIgRhrDnNSm_M7Y.about: James Hazard Wilson II, born in 1800, was one of many children born to his parents, James Hazard Wilson Sr. and Ruth Davidson Wilson. The Wilson family arrived in America from Ireland in the mid-1700s and followed the migration trail down through the Carolinas to finally settle in Tennessee by the late 1700s. In March of 1821, James Hazard Wilson II married his cousin, Emeline Wilson, which was a common practice before the turn of the 20th century. Prominent Tennessee and Texas historical figure, Sam Houston, served as the best man at his wedding. Not long after, James II and Emeline were ready to put down roots. Having grown up in Williamson County, James II could think of no better place to call home and raise a family. They purchased hundreds of acres of land to establish their plantation and began construction on the Ravenswood house in 1825. As was the case with most southern plantations during this time period, it was likely that the land was cleared, the materials were fashioned, and the house was built by the hands of those enslaved. In 1830, the first census following the completion of Ravenswood, the Wilson family was counted as having five people enslaved at Ravenswood. The number of people it would take to complete such a large undertaking to build a house would require a far greater number. ChIJYVB4-XFmZIgRLZRnwJ3d0JU.home: We are an entrepreneurial community of retail, dining, art, and entertainment businesses in Nashville’s vibrant Wedgewood-Houston neighborhood. At Houston Station, a historic landmark, you'll discover unique, authentic Nashville local shops, acclaimed restaurants, and prime retail and office space for lease—all within a dynamic environment of creativity and inspiration. Interested in learning more about available spaces? CALL 615-504-7406 or FILL OUT THE FORM BELOW.
ChIJYVB4-XFmZIgRLZRnwJ3d0JU.about: Around 1900, the developing Wedgewood-Houston Neighborhood saw the construction of two factories side by side. The brick and heavy timber factory at 434 Houston Street was home to the American Syrup Company, where syrups, jams, and jellies were made under a variety of labels, including Bagwell Preserves, featuring Jambo the Bear as its mascot. Upstairs, tobacco was brought by local farmers for processing and distribution across the country by rail. Our sister building at 438 Houston Street was the original home of the May Hosiery Mill, where socks and ladies’ stockings were primary products. Bomb fuses were produced during the war years, and parachutes of silk during WWI, and of nylon during WWII. The May Hosiery Company also sponsored numerous Jewish refugees who survived by fleeing Hitler’s Germany to Nashville where they were guaranteed employment and residency required by the U.S. for emigration. Over the second half of the twentieth century, the Wedgewood/Houston neighborhood declined. Factories closed and many buildings became vacant. A resurgence began to build momentum around 2010, and today the area is seeing a vibrant and energetic redevelopment. Houston Station has been an integral part of this story. Today Houston Station is home to two restaurants, a coffee house, and twenty other assorted retail and office businesses spanning creative music, art, and entertainment

He understands how images drive the stories of our age and seeks to capture exceptional visuals that convey an idea at a glance. My life has often included an interesting juxtaposition of opposites. I began my career covering art openings, charity fundraisers, debutante balls, and fashion shows for the society pages of the Pittsburgh Tribune-Review. At the same time I would also sneak my camera into rock clubs, lounges and concert venues to shoot both local bands and nationally touring acts. ChIJfaA-dTh6ZIgRbMjDb2ROCiE.about: Explore the history of the Cool Springs House in Brentwood, Tennessee. The Cool Springs House and the land upon which it was originally located was closely associated with the Barfield and Carothers families, both pioneer families in the Brentwood area. Lewis Barfield came to Williamson County in the early 1800s from North Carolina. In 1818, his daughter, Penelope Barfield, married James Carothers, the son of Robert Carothers, who held one of the original Revolutionary War Land Grants in the Brentwood area. The Carothers family prospered, acquiring a large amount of land. The original two log rooms, front staircase, and large upstairs room of the Cool Springs House were built in the 1830s. It was one of the largest log homes in middle Tennessee at the time. The original house was located at what is presently the intersection of Mallory Lane and Cool Springs Boulevard. At the death of James Carothers, the home was later passed to their son, Dr. Robert Blake Carothers. The first of Robert Carothers’ six wives was Margaret Jane Crockett. She was a cousin to Andrew Crockett III who owned the land where the house is currently located in Crockett Park. The original log house underwent major additions and renovations in the later 1870s while still under the ownership of Dr. Carothers. During this renovation, they added the downstairs halls, front porch, and additional rooms upstairs.

ChIJz9O2ZHn4Y4gReIGtLUpFKM0.about: The earliest known photograph of Oaklands Mansion was taken in the winter time, circa 1888, and reads “Mr. George Darrow’s residence.” Oaklands began in the late eighteen teens when Dr. James Maney and his wife Sallie Murfree Maney moved to Murfreesboro. In 1813, Sallie inherited 274 acres of land north of the town named for her father, Colonel Hardy Murfree. The Maney family then migrated from Maney’s Neck, NC, to Middle Tennessee in the mid Eighteen-teens, forcibly moving twenty-three enslaved individuals with them as well. About three generations of enslaved families would eventually live, work, and die at Oaklands. A document from the Williamson County Probate notes that the Maney’s brought the following enslaved individuals with them from North Carolina: It was on this tract that the Maneys constructed what would become one of the most elegant homes in Middle Tennessee. The original structure built on this land was a two-room brick house next to a large spring north of Murfreesboro and was built by enslaved people owned by the Maneys. The two-room house was built on the hall-and-parlor plan, a design that would have been familiar to the Maneys. It was a well-constructed one-and-a-half-story house with dormer windows and a chimney at each end, as well as penciling on the brick mortar to enhance the house’s apperance.
